packet.headline_seed: After banning foreign routers, FCC says existing ones can get updates until 2029
packet.description_seed: The Federal Communications Commission is relenting a bit on its restrictive router rules, saying it will allow foreign-made routers to receive software and firmware updates until at least January 1, 2029. The FCC also expanded the waiver to cover more types of software updates. Previously, the FCC said routers currently on the market or already sold to consumers could receive security patches and other updates only until March 1, 2027. On Friday, the agency announced a waiver extension that lets devices receive updates until January 1, 2029, and said the waiver may eventually become permanent. The software-update cutoff date is part of a sweeping set of rules the FCC announced in March. Claiming that restrictions are needed for national security reasons, the FCC imposed a ban on new hardware and related limits on software updates for routers that were authorized for sale before the ban was implemented. The Federal Communications Commission is relenting a bit on its restrictive router rules, saying it will allow foreign-made routers to receive software and firmware updates until at least January 1, 2029. The FCC also expanded the waiver to cover more types of software updates. Previously, the FCC said routers currently on the market or already sold to consumers could receive security patches and other updates only until March 1, 2027. On Friday, the agency announced a waiver extension that lets devices receive updates until January 1, 2029, and said the waiver may eventually become permanent.

The software-update cutoff date is part of a sweeping set of rules the FCC announced in March. Claiming that restrictions are needed for national security reasons, the FCC imposed a ban on new hardware and related limits on software updates for routers that were authorized for sale before the ban was implemented. Specifically, the FCC said in March that it would stop approving consumer-grade routers made outside the US, an action that affects virtually every router maker (with the possible exception of Starlink). The Trump administration is handing out exemptions to hardware makers that it decides are safe enough, with Netgear and the Amazon-owned Eero among those receiving exemptions so far.

The hardware ban is only for new devices, so all routers previously approved for sale in the US can continue to be imported and sold without obtaining a special exemption. But previously approved routers were hit with a separate rule that would prohibit software and firmware updates—unless the FCC keeps extending the cutoff date after which no updates can be installed. The new 2029 cutoff date announced Friday applies to foreign-made routers and foreign-made drones, which were both added to the Covered List. Devices on the Covered List “are deemed to pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States or the security and safety of United States persons,” the FCC says.

[Lähde: Ars Technica]
The Federal Communications Commission is relenting a bit on its restrictive router rules, saying it will allow foreign-made routers to receive software and firmware updates until at least January 1, 2029. The FCC also expanded the waiver to cover more types of software updates.

Previously, the FCC said routers currently on the market or already sold to consumers could receive security patches and other updates only until March 1, 2027. On Friday, the agency announced a waiver extension that lets devices receive updates until January 1, 2029, and said the waiver may eventually become permanent.

The software-update cutoff date is part of a sweeping set of rules the FCC announced in March. Claiming that restrictions are needed for national security reasons, the FCC imposed a ban on new hardware and related limits on software updates for routers that were authorized for sale before the ban was implemented.

Specifically, the FCC said in March that it would stop approving consumer-grade routers made outside the US, an action that affects virtually every router maker (with the possible exception of Starlink). The Trump administration is handing out exemptions to hardware makers that it decides are safe enough, with Netgear and the Amazon-owned Eero among those receiving exemptions so far.

The hardware ban is only for new devices, so all routers previously approved for sale in the US can continue to be imported and sold without obtaining a special exemption. But previously approved routers were hit with a separate rule that would prohibit software and firmware updates—unless the FCC keeps extending the cutoff date after which no updates can be installed.

The new 2029 cutoff date announced Friday applies to foreign-made routers and foreign-made drones, which were both added to the Covered List. Devices on the Covered List “are deemed to pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States or the security and safety of United States persons,” the FCC says.

The United States’ foreign router ban didn’t make a whole lot of sense, and today may not change that. The FCC has just granted Netgear a conditional approval to import its future consumer routers, cable modems, and cable gateways into the US through October 1st, 2027 — even though the company builds those devices in Asia and has not announced any plan to bring manufacturing to the United States.

Neither the FCC’s announcement nor Netgear’s announcement explain why Netgear was granted the temporary exemption. The FCC only states that the Pentagon has now made “a specific determination” that “such devices do not pose risks to U.S. national security.”

That’s strange, given how the FCC’s original and exceptionally loose justification for the entire router ban was that foreign routers automatically pose a national security threat because of incidents like Volt Typhoon, where Netgear routers were among those primarily targeted by the Chinese hacking group. (The issue was arguably US telecom companies and router owners not following basic security best practices like updating firmware and changing default passwords, not the routers themselves.)

payload.title: FCC jatkaa ulkomaisten reitittimien päivityslupaa vuoteen 2029
payload.summary: Yhdysvaltain viestintäviranomainen FCC sallii aiemmin hyväksyttyjen ulkomailla valmistettujen reitittimien ohjelmisto- ja laiteohjelmistopäivitykset ainakin 1. tammikuuta 2029 saakka.
payload.content:
Yhdysvaltain viestintäviranomainen FCC on lieventänyt ulkomailla valmistettuja reitittimiä koskevia rajoituksiaan: jo markkinoilla olevat tai aiemmin myyntiin hyväksytyt laitteet voivat saada ohjelmisto- ja laiteohjelmistopäivityksiä ainakin 1. tammikuuta 2029 saakka. Aiempi takaraja olisi katkaissut tällaisten laitteiden tietoturva- ja muut päivitykset 1. maaliskuuta 2027.

## Päivityksille lisää aikaa

FCC ilmoitti perjantaina jatkavansa poikkeuslupaa, joka koskee ulkomailla valmistettuja reitittimiä. Virasto myös laajensi poikkeuksen kattamaan aiempaa useampia ohjelmistopäivitysten tyyppejä. Käytännössä muutos antaa kuluttajille, jälleenmyyjille ja laitevalmistajille pidemmän siirtymäajan ennen kuin päivitysrajoitukset voisivat tulla voimaan.

Uusi päivämäärä ei koske vain reitittimiä, vaan myös ulkomailla valmistettuja droneja, jotka on lisätty Yhdysvaltojen niin sanotulle Covered List -listalle. Listalle kuuluvien laitteiden katsotaan FCC:n mukaan aiheuttavan hyväksymättömän riskin Yhdysvaltojen kansalliselle turvallisuudelle tai Yhdysvalloissa olevien henkilöiden turvallisuudelle.

## Kielto koskee uusia laitteita

Maaliskuussa ilmoitettu laajempi sääntelypaketti rajoittaa erityisesti uusien kuluttajatason reitittimien hyväksymistä, jos ne on valmistettu Yhdysvaltojen ulkopuolella. FCC perustelee rajoituksia kansallisen turvallisuuden tarpeilla. Päätös vaikuttaa laajasti reititinvalmistajiin, sillä suuri osa kuluttajamarkkinoiden laitteista valmistetaan Yhdysvaltojen ulkopuolella.

Tärkeä rajaus on, että laitteistokielto koskee uusia laitteita. Reitittimet, jotka on jo hyväksytty myyntiin Yhdysvalloissa ennen kiellon voimaantuloa, voivat edelleen olla maahantuonnissa ja myynnissä ilman erillistä poikkeusta. Niitä koski kuitenkin erillinen päivityssääntö, jonka mukaan ohjelmisto- ja laiteohjelmistopäivitykset olisivat myöhemmin estyneet, ellei FCC jatka määräaikaa.

## Poikkeuksista voi tulla pysyviä

FCC:n mukaan nykyinen jatko voi myöhemmin muuttua pysyväksi. Samalla Yhdysvaltain hallinto on alkanut myöntää poikkeuksia valmistajille, joita se pitää riittävän turvallisina. Tähän mennessä poikkeuksen saaneiden joukossa ovat Netgear ja Amazonin omistama Eero.

Päätös ei siis poista varsinaista uutta laitekieltoa, mutta se vähentää välitöntä riskiä siitä, että jo käytössä olevat reitittimet jäisivät ilman tietoturvapäivityksiä vuoden 2027 jälkeen.

The Federal Communications Commission is relenting a bit on its restrictive router rules, saying it will allow foreign-made routers to receive software and firmware updates until at least January 1, 2029. The FCC also expanded the waiver to cover more types of software updates. Previously, the FCC said routers currently on the market or already sold to consumers could receive security patches and other updates only until March 1, 2027. On Friday, the agency announced a waiver extension that lets devices receive updates until January 1, 2029, and said the waiver may eventually become permanent.

The software-update cutoff date is part of a sweeping set of rules the FCC announced in March. Claiming that restrictions are needed for national security reasons, the FCC imposed a ban on new hardware and related limits on software updates for routers that were authorized for sale before the ban was implemented. Specifically, the FCC said in March that it would stop approving consumer-grade routers made outside the US, an action that affects virtually every router maker (with the possible exception of Starlink). The Trump administration is handing out exemptions to hardware makers that it decides are safe enough, with Netgear and the Amazon-owned Eero among those receiving exemptions so far.

The hardware ban is only for new devices, so all routers previously approved for sale in the US can continue to be imported and sold without obtaining a special exemption. But previously approved routers were hit with a separate rule that would prohibit software and firmware updates—unless the FCC keeps extending the cutoff date after which no updates can be installed. The new 2029 cutoff date announced Friday applies to foreign-made routers and foreign-made drones, which were both added to the Covered List. Devices on the Covered List “are deemed to pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States or the security and safety of United States persons,” the FCC says.
